steps.body:
Words carry grouping, and the wrong words change the expression.

3(n + 2) is read *three times the **sum** of n and 2* — the bracket is one object, and the 3 multiplies all of it. Say instead *three times n, plus 2* and you have described 3n + 2, a different expression entirely.
Build the one the words describe.

widget.prompt: Build 'three times the sum of x and 2': three groups, each holding one x and two units.
widget.successFeedback: 3x + 6. Each of the three groups carried its own 2, so the units came to six. That is 3(x + 2) — the bracket travelled with the multiplication.
widget.xFeedback: Check the x-tiles: three groups means three x-tiles.
widget.constFeedback: Check the unit tiles: each of the three groups holds 2, so six in all — not two.

explanationVariants: 'The sum of x and 5, doubled' groups the sum first, then doubles it: 2(x + 5).
Doubling applies to the whole sum, so the sum needs a bracket.

widget.prompt: Which expression is 'the sum of x and 5, doubled'?

options.label: 2(x + 5)
options.feedback: The sum is formed first and the doubling applies to all of it.

options.label: 2x + 5
options.feedback: This doubles only the x. The phrase doubles the whole sum.

options.label: x + 10
options.feedback: This doubles only the 5 and leaves the x alone — the phrase doubles the whole sum, both parts together.

options.label: 2x + 10x
options.feedback: This is not equivalent to either reading; it simplifies to 12x.

explanationVariants: 4n − 1 is 'one less than four times n' — the multiplication happens first, then 1 is removed.
There is no bracket, so the 4 reaches only the n.

options.label: one less than four times n
options.feedback: 4n is formed first, then 1 is subtracted from it.

options.label: four times one less than n
four less than n
options.feedback: That would be n − 4, which subtracts 4 from n. Here n is multiplied by 4 first, and only 1 is taken away.

options.label: one less than n, times four
options.feedback: That is 4(n − 1) again — the words put the subtraction inside a group.

steps.body:
The bracket also lets you treat a whole expression as a **single entity**.

In 3(n + 2) you can view (n + 2) as one thing being tripled, without ever looking inside it. That view is what makes 3(n + 2) + 4(n + 2) = 7(n + 2) obvious — seven of the same object — no distributing required.
Two of one object, plus three more.

widget.prompt: Build 5(x + 1): five groups, each with one x and one unit.
widget.successFeedback: 5x + 5. Seen the other way, this is five copies of the single object (x + 1) — which is why 2(x + 1) + 3(x + 1) would come to exactly this.
widget.xFeedback: Check the x-tiles: five groups, one x each.
widget.constFeedback: Check the unit tiles: five groups, one unit each.

steps.body: Count the objects instead of expanding.
explanationVariants: 2(y + 3) + 5(y + 3) is 2 of the object plus 5 of it, so 7(y + 3).
Treat (y + 3) as a single thing: 2 + 5 = 7 of them.

widget.prompt: 2(y + 3) + 5(y + 3) equals ?(y + 3). What number goes in the blank?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 multiplies 2 and 5. Here they are being ADDED — two of the object plus five more makes seven.
3 is inside the bracket, not a count of the objects. Count the copies: 2 + 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Treating (y + 3) as one object: 2 of them plus 5 of them is 7 of them.

steps.body: Words into symbols, with the grouping doing real work.
explanationVariants: 'Five times the sum of a number and 4' is 5(n + 4); distributed that is 5n + 20.
The sum is grouped first, so the 5 reaches both the n and the 4.
hints: Which part of the phrase is grouped? Look for the word 'sum'.
The sum of a number and 4 is (n + 4), and five times it is 5(n + 4).
Distributing gives 5n + 20 — the 5 reaches the 4 as well.

widget.prompt: 'Five times the sum of a number and 4' — which pair of forms is correct?

options.label: 5(n + 4), which equals 5n + 20
options.feedback: The sum is grouped, so the 5 multiplies both parts.

options.label: 5n + 4, which equals 5(n + 4)
options.feedback: These two are not equal: 5n + 4 leaves the 4 untouched by the 5.

options.label: 5(n + 4), which equals 5n + 4
options.feedback: The first form is right but distributing must reach the 4: 5 × 4 = 20.

options.label: n + 20, which equals 5(n + 4)
options.feedback: n + 20 only multiplies the 4 by five and leaves n alone.

steps.body: Say it precisely and the symbols follow.
takeaways: 'The sum of' groups what follows — that is where brackets come from.
3(n + 2) and 3n + 2 are different expressions, and the words tell them apart.
A bracket can be viewed as one object, which makes counting copies easier than expanding.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: equivalent expressions, and how to prove two of them really do match.
